ranking.rationale: Age is one of the strongest and most stable predictors of cholesterol status in NHANES, with a direct biological relationship that should generalize across domains better than survey-year, birthplace, marital status, missingness indicators, or diagnosis-history shortcuts.

Sex is a strong, biologically stable determinant of cholesterol patterns and adds major complementary signal beyond age. It is more semantically robust across NHANES domains than survey year, birthplace, education, marital status, missingness indicators, or diagnosis-history variables that can reflect access-to-care, reporting behavior, or domain shifts.

Diabetes history is a strong, biologically plausible correlate of dyslipidemia/cholesterol that should remain predictive across NHANES domains, adding substantial stable signal beyond age and sex while avoiding direct domain identifiers like survey year or birthplace and being less brittle than missingness/refusal indicators.

Hypertension history is a strong, biologically plausible correlate of dyslipidemia and cardiovascular-metabolic risk that should remain predictive across NHANES domains. It adds stable health-status information beyond age, sex, and diabetes, while avoiding brittle domain indicators like survey year or country-of-birth and being more directly relevant than weaker comorbidity or socioeconomic proxies.

A negative diabetes-history indicator adds strong, semantically stable cardiovascular-metabolic signal beyond age, sex, hypertension, and diabetes-yes. It is more robust than year, birthplace, education, marital status, or missing/refusal codes, which are more likely to encode domain or access-to-care artifacts.

Kidney disease history adds clinically meaningful, likely domain-stable cardiovascular risk information beyond age, sex, hypertension, and diabetes. The 'No kidney failure' indicator is preferable to demographic or year features that may encode domain shifts, and more useful than rare/refusal categories or redundant missingness flags.

Kidney disease history is a clinically stable correlate of dyslipidemia and cardiovascular-metabolic risk, adding useful signal beyond age, sex, diabetes, hypertension, and the already selected kidney-no indicator. It is more semantically robust than demographic or year features and less likely to encode domain shift than missing/refused categories.

Prediabetes/no-prediabetes status adds stable metabolic risk information for cholesterol beyond age, sex, diabetes, hypertension, and kidney disease. The explicit negative category is likely common and informative, while being less domain-specific and less brittle than survey year, birthplace, education, marital status, or missing/refusal indicators.

Hypertension history is a strong, semantically stable cardiometabolic correlate of cholesterol risk and adds useful signal beyond age, sex, diabetes, kidney disease, and prediabetes. The explicit non-hypertension category is likely more informative than missing/refused indicators and avoids brittle domain-ID features like survey year or birthplace.

Dialysis history is a strong, semantically stable marker of severe kidney/metabolic disease and cardiovascular risk, which is plausibly associated with abnormal cholesterol beyond age, sex, hypertension, diabetes, prediabetes, and kidney-disease history already selected. It adds clinically meaningful signal while avoiding obvious domain-ID features like survey year or birthplace and is less likely than socioeconomic or marital-status variables to act as a brittle demographic shortcut.

Prediabetes history adds clinically relevant, semantically stable signal for cholesterol risk beyond age, sex, diabetes, hypertension, and kidney disease. It is more transportable than demographic or survey-year features and more informative than refusal/missing indicators or redundant alternate categories from already selected variables.

Arthritis history adds stable health-status signal beyond age, sex, diabetes, hypertension, and kidney disease. It is plausibly associated with systemic inflammation, reduced activity, obesity, and medication patterns that relate to cholesterol, while being less likely than birthplace, education, marital status, missingness flags, or survey year to encode domain shifts or demographic shortcuts.

Arthritis absence adds useful complementary health-status signal beyond age, sex, diabetes, hypertension, kidney disease, and arthritis presence already selected. It is more semantically tied to chronic metabolic/inflammatory risk than demographic or survey-year variables, and is preferable to missing/refused indicators or nhanes_year, which are more likely to encode domain shift artifacts.

Dialysis status adds strong, semantically stable cardiovascular/metabolic risk information relevant to cholesterol beyond age, sex, diabetes, hypertension, kidney disease, and arthritis. It is more clinically informative and less likely to act as a domain or demographic shortcut than education, marital status, birthplace, missingness, or survey year.

Education adds stable socioeconomic signal beyond age, sex, and existing cardiometabolic comorbidities, and is more likely to generalize across NHANES domains than year, birthplace, marital status, or refusal/missing indicators. Lower educational attainment is plausibly associated with cholesterol risk through diet, healthcare access, and chronic disease burden, giving good marginal value without being an obvious domain identifier.

College-or-above education adds stable socioeconomic signal beyond age, sex, diabetes, hypertension, kidney disease, arthritis, and low-education already selected. Education is semantically linked to diet, healthcare access, and chronic disease risk relevant to cholesterol, while being less direct domain-identifying than survey year or birthplace and less brittle than missing/refused indicators.

Education is already proving useful, and adding the next adjacent schooling level should improve the socioeconomic gradient signal for cholesterol risk beyond the currently selected low/high education indicators. This is more semantically stable across NHANES domains than year, birthplace, marital-status, or missing/refusal indicators, and likely adds more marginal value than rare disease or nonresponse categories.

Adds the remaining major education level signal, which is a broadly stable socioeconomic predictor of cholesterol-related risk and healthcare patterns across domains. Adds the remaining substantive education level category, which is a stable socioeconomic predictor of cholesterol-related risk and healthcare patterns across domains. It complements the already selected education indicators better than missing/refused codes or nhanes_year, which are more likely to encode domain shift or survey artifacts.

It is more semantically predictive and less likely to act as a domain identifier than year, birthplace, marital status, or missing/refused indicators.

Adds the complementary psoriasis-positive indicator for an already useful inflammatory comorbidity signal; this is more semantically tied to cholesterol risk and likely more stable across domains than missing/refused codes, marital/birth variables, or nhanes_year, which may encode domain shift.

It is less likely than survey year or missing/refused indicators to encode domain shift directly, and offers more robust marginal value than additional rare-response categories.
